::: {.solutions}

Five real Paper 2 questions you got wrong across the **2022** and **2023** papers (Q6–Q10). Every one is a
*reasoning* question: a proof error, a quantifier order, a converse that quietly turns out true, a
solution-count preserved under a reflection, a geometry count that is **always** the same. Each solution says
**why**, flags the exact slip, and links to the full mark scheme and the toolkit session that drills it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The five slips these test

- **Irreducible ≠ prime value** (2022 Q7): a polynomial not factorising says nothing about whether the
  *number* it produces is prime.
- **Quantifier order** (2022 Q10): "for each $x$ there is an $n$" (the $n$ may depend on $x$) is very
  different from "one $n$ works for all $x$".
- **Reflection preserves the count** (2023 Q6): $y=\log_a x$ is $y=a^x$ mirrored in $y=x$, so each meets the
  line $y=x$ the same number of times.
- **Count is always 3** (2023 Q8): every non-right triangle has *exactly* three dividing lines — so "exactly
  1" and "exactly 2" are impossible.
- **A converse can be true** (2023 Q9): the statement is false, but its converse is forced true by a hidden
  average.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Answer form.** MCQ → one letter. All answer letters are the **official** ones; each links to the full
worked solution in that paper's **[Mark scheme](../2022_paper2/class_material.qmd)**.
:::

# 2022 Paper 2

## Question 7

::: {.question}
Consider the claim: *the difference between two consecutive positive cube numbers is always prime.* Here is an
attempted proof:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $(x+1)^{3}=x^{3}+3x^{2}+3x+1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; Taking $x$ a positive integer, the difference of consecutive cubes is $(x+1)^{3}-x^{3}=3x^{2}+3x+1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; It is impossible to factorise $3x^{2}+3x+1$ into two linear factors with integer coefficients, because its discriminant is negative.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** &nbsp; Therefore for every positive integer value of $x$, the integer $3x^{2}+3x+1$ cannot be factorised.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**V** &nbsp; Hence the difference between two consecutive cube numbers will always be prime.

Which best describes this proof? &nbsp; **A** correct, claim true &nbsp; **B** correct, but counterexamples
exist &nbsp; **C** first error line I &nbsp; **D** line II &nbsp; **E** line III &nbsp; **F** line IV &nbsp;
**G** line V
:::

Look for the **first** line that does not follow. Lines I–III are fine; watch the jump from *polynomial* to
[*integer value*]{.hl} at IV.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — F (first error on line IV)

[*(answer F)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — spot the first error in a "difference of cubes is prime" proof · **spot the error (S7)**
:::


- **Line III is true:** the *polynomial* $3x^{2}+3x+1$ has discriminant $9-12=-3<0$, so it does not split into
  integer linear factors — it is **irreducible**.
- **Line IV is the false leap:** "the polynomial doesn't factorise, so the **number** $3x^{2}+3x+1$ can never
  be factorised (is prime)." Irreducible polynomial $\neq$ prime values. **Counterexample:** $x=5$ gives
  $3(25)+15+1=91=7\times13$ — composite. (This is the difference $6^{3}-5^{3}=91$.)
- **Line V is *not* the first error:** it follows correctly *from* IV (if the value could never be factorised
  it would indeed always be prime). The error was already made at IV.

*Your slip: you picked **G (line V)** — the conclusion looks wrong, so it seems the guilty line. But V is a
valid deduction from IV; the flaw is the polynomial-to-number jump at **IV**. **Full solution:
[2022 P2 MS · Q7](../2022_paper2/class_material.qmd). Toolkit: [S7](../../toolkit/s07_assignment_ms.qmd),
[S5 — factorisation ⇒ primality](../../toolkit/s05_concepts.qmd).***
:::

## Question 10

::: {.question}
Which of the following statements is/are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; For **all** real numbers $x$ and for **all** positive integers $n$, $\;x<n$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; For **all** real numbers $x$, **there exists** a positive integer $n$ such that $\;x<n$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; **There exists** a real number $x$ such that for **all** positive integers $n$, $\;x<n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp; **E** I and II only
&nbsp; **F** I and III only &nbsp; **G** II and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

The whole question is **which quantifier comes first**: in II the $n$ may [depend on $x$]{.hl}; in III one
$x$ must beat **every** $n$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — G (II and III only)

[*(answer G)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — the order of quantifiers · **quantifiers (S4)**
:::


- **I — false.** It claims *every* real is below *every* positive integer. Take $x=100,\ n=1$: $100<1$ is
  false.
- **II — true.** For each real $x$ you may choose an $n$ **depending on $x$**: take $n=\lfloor x\rfloor+1$
  (or $n=1$ if $x<1$). A positive integer larger than any given $x$ always exists.
- **III — true.** You need **one** real $x$ below *all* positive integers: take $x=0$ (indeed any $x\le0$).
  Then $x<n$ for every positive integer $n$.

So II and III hold — **G**.

*Your slip: you doubted **II**. "$\forall x\,\exists n$" only asks that **some** $n$ work for each $x$, and a
different $n$ for a different $x$ is allowed — that is exactly the Archimedean property. Do not confuse it
with I ("one statement for all $x,n$ at once"). **Full solution: [2022 P2 MS · Q10](../2022_paper2/class_material.qmd).
Toolkit: [S4 — quantifiers & order](../../toolkit/s04_concepts.qmd).***
:::

# 2023 Paper 2

## Question 6

::: {.question}
Let $a$ be real with $a>1$, and consider $(*)$: $\;a^{x}=x$. Which of the following equations **must** have the
**same number** of real solutions as $(*)$, for every such $a$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $\log_a x=x$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **II** &nbsp; $a^{2x}=x^{2}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **III** &nbsp; $a^{2x}=2x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp; **E** I and II only
&nbsp; **F** I and III only &nbsp; **G** II and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

$(*)$ itself has $0$, $1$ or $2$ solutions depending on $a$. For each option, ask whether it always matches
that count — a [reflection or a substitution]{.hl} keeps the count; an extra branch changes it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — F (I and III only)

[*(answer F)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — which equations share the solution-count of $a^{x}=x$ · **graphs of exp / log**
:::


- **I ($\log_a x=x$) — same count.** $y=\log_a x$ is the reflection of $y=a^{x}$ in the line $y=x$. Since
  $y=x$ is the mirror itself, the points where $y=a^{x}$ meets $y=x$ reflect **one-to-one** onto the points
  where $y=\log_a x$ meets $y=x$. Same number, always. ✔
- **II ($a^{2x}=x^{2}$) — different count.** $a^{2x}=(a^{x})^{2}=x^{2}\Leftrightarrow a^{x}=\lvert x\rvert$,
  i.e. $a^{x}=x$ (for $x\ge0$) **or** $a^{x}=-x$ (for $x<0$). The extra branch $a^{x}=-x$ always has
  **exactly one** solution, so II has *one more* solution than $(*)$. ✘
- **III ($a^{2x}=2x$) — same count.** Put $u=2x$: it becomes $a^{u}=u$, the very form of $(*)$, and $x\mapsto
  2x$ is a bijection. Same number, always. ✔

So I and III — **F**.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "y=aˣ and y=log_a x are reflections in y=x, so each meets the line y=x the same number of times (here a=1.4: two intersections each, mirrored). Equation II adds the branch aˣ=−x (one extra solution)."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
a=1.4
x=np.linspace(-1,6,400); xp=np.linspace(0.03,6,400)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2,4.4))
ax.plot(x,a**x,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2,label='y=aˣ')
ax.plot(xp,np.log(xp)/np.log(a),color='#dd6b20',lw=2,label='y=log_a x')
ax.plot(x,x,color='0.5',ls='--',lw=1.2,label='y=x')
# intersections of a^x=x
from scipy.optimize import brentq
r1=brentq(lambda t:a**t-t,1.5,3); r2=brentq(lambda t:a**t-t,3,6)
for r in (r1,r2):
    ax.plot(r,r,'o',color='#2b6cb0',ms=6); ax.plot(r,r,'o',mfc='none',mec='#dd6b20',ms=11)
ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.set_xlim(-1,6); ax.set_ylim(-1,6)
ax.axhline(0,color='0.8',lw=.6); ax.axvline(0,color='0.8',lw=.6)
ax.legend(fontsize=8,loc='upper left'); ax.set_xlabel('x'); ax.set_ylabel('y')
ax.set_title('I: same intersections with y=x, mirrored',fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

*Your slip: you excluded **I**, thinking the domain $x>0$ of $\log_a x$ changes the count. But $a^{x}=x$
already forces $x>0$ (since $a^{x}>0$), so no solution is lost — the reflection is exact. **Full solution:
[2023 P2 MS · Q6](../2023_paper2/class_material.qmd).***
:::

## Question 8

::: {.question}
A student draws a triangle that is acute-angled or obtuse-angled but **not** right-angled, and counts the
straight lines that divide it into two triangles, **at least one** of which is right-angled. Which is/are
true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; A triangle can be drawn with exactly **1** such line.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; … exactly **2** such lines.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; … exactly **3** such lines.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp; **E** I and II only
&nbsp; **F** I and III only &nbsp; **G** II and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

Such a line is a **cevian** (vertex to the opposite side). A right angle appears either at its **foot** (the
line is an *altitude* — valid only if the foot lands inside the side) or at the **vertex** (the line makes
$90^\circ$ with a side there — possible only where the [angle exceeds $90^\circ$]{.hl}).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — D (III only)

[*(answer D)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — count the lines splitting a triangle into two, one right-angled · **geometry reasoning**
:::


Count the valid lines for each shape:

- **Acute triangle:** all three **altitudes** have their feet **inside** the opposite side, and each splits
  the triangle into two right-angled triangles → **3 lines**. No angle exceeds $90^\circ$, so there are no
  vertex-right-angle lines. Exactly **3**.
- **Obtuse triangle** (obtuse at $V$): only the altitude **from $V$** has an interior foot (the other two
  altitudes' feet fall *outside* the triangle) → **1**; and at the obtuse vertex $V$ you can draw **two**
  cevians making $90^\circ$ with each of its sides → **2**. Total **3**.

So **every** allowed triangle has **exactly 3** such lines. Hence a triangle with exactly $3$ exists (III
true), but **none** with exactly $1$ or exactly $2$ (I, II false) — **D**.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Both cases give exactly 3 dividing lines. Left (acute): the three altitudes, feet inside each side. Right (obtuse at C): the altitude from C plus two cevians from C that make a right angle with CA and CB."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
def foot(V,P,Q):
    P=np.array(P,float);Q=np.array(Q,float);V=np.array(V,float)
    t=((V-P)@(Q-P))/((Q-P)@(Q-P)); return P+t*(Q-P)
def perp_to_side_hit(C,S,P,Q):
    # cevian from C perpendicular to side CS (S a vertex), hitting line PQ (the base y=0 here)
    C=np.array(C,float);S=np.array(S,float)
    d=S-C; dirp=np.array([-d[1],d[0]])
    if dirp[1]>0: dirp=-dirp           # point downward toward base
    t=(0-C[1])/dirp[1]; return C+t*dirp
fig,(ax1,ax2)=plt.subplots(2,1,figsize=(5.0,7.2))
# acute
A,B,C=np.array([0,0]),np.array([4,0]),np.array([1.6,2.7])
tri=np.array([A,B,C,A]); ax1.plot(tri[:,0],tri[:,1],'k',lw=2)
for V,P,Q in [(A,B,C),(B,A,C),(C,A,B)]:
    ax1.plot([V[0],foot(V,P,Q)[0]],[V[1],foot(V,P,Q)[1]],color='#2b6cb0',lw=1.6)
    ax1.plot(*foot(V,P,Q),'o',color='#dd6b20',ms=4)
ax1.set_title('Acute: 3 altitudes',fontsize=10); ax1.set_aspect('equal'); ax1.axis('off')
# obtuse at C
A,B,C=np.array([0,0]),np.array([5,0]),np.array([0.5,1.3])
tri=np.array([A,B,C,A]); ax2.plot(tri[:,0],tri[:,1],'k',lw=2)
ax2.plot([C[0],foot(C,A,B)[0]],[C[1],foot(C,A,B)[1]],color='#2b6cb0',lw=1.6)   # altitude from C
for S in (A,B):
    D=perp_to_side_hit(C,S,A,B)
    ax2.plot([C[0],D[0]],[C[1],D[1]],color='#2ca02c',lw=1.6)
    ax2.plot(*D,'o',color='#2ca02c',ms=4)
ax2.plot(*foot(C,A,B),'o',color='#dd6b20',ms=4)
ax2.set_title('Obtuse at C: 1 altitude + 2 cevians',fontsize=10); ax2.set_aspect('equal'); ax2.axis('off')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

*Your slip: you picked **H (I, II and III)**, assuming $1$, $2$ and $3$ are all reachable. The count is
**always** $3$, so only III can happen. **Full solution: [2023 P2 MS · Q8](../2023_paper2/class_material.qmd).***
:::

## Question 9

::: {.question}
Consider the statement about a pentagon $P$:

&nbsp;&nbsp;$(*)$ &nbsp; *If at least one of the interior angles in $P$ is $108^\circ$, then all the interior
angles in $P$ form an arithmetic sequence.*

Which of the following is/are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; The statement $(*)$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; The contrapositive of $(*)$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; The converse of $(*)$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp; **E** I and II only
&nbsp; **F** I and III only &nbsp; **G** II and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

A statement and its **contrapositive** always share a truth value; the **converse** is independent — test it
by [writing the arithmetic sequence out]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — D (III only)

[*(answer D)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — a statement, its contrapositive, and its converse · **converse & contrapositive (S2)**
:::


- **I — $(*)$ is false.** Angles of a pentagon sum to $540^\circ$. Take $100^\circ,102^\circ,108^\circ,110^\circ,120^\circ$
  (sum $540^\circ$): one angle is $108^\circ$, yet $100,102,108,110,120$ is **not** an arithmetic sequence
  (differences $2,6,2,10$). So $(*)$ fails.
- **II — the contrapositive is false too.** A statement and its contrapositive are **logically equivalent**,
  so it has the same (false) truth value as $(*)$.
- **III — the converse is true.** Converse: *"if all interior angles form an arithmetic sequence, then at
  least one is $108^\circ$."* Write the five angles as $a-2d,\,a-d,\,a,\,a+d,\,a+2d$; their sum is $5a=540^\circ$,
  so $a=108^\circ$. The **middle** angle is $108^\circ$ — so at least one angle is $108^\circ$. ✔

Only III — **D**.

*Your slip: you picked **A (none)**, assuming all three fail. The converse is forced true because a $5$-term
arithmetic sequence summing to $540^\circ$ has middle term $540/5=108$. Always check a converse by building
the object, not by guessing. **Full solution: [2023 P2 MS · Q9](../2023_paper2/class_material.qmd).
Toolkit: [S2 — converse & contrapositive](../../toolkit/s02_concepts.qmd).***
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What to take away

- **Proof errors:** the first error is the earliest line that doesn't follow — a valid deduction *from* a
  false line (2022 Q7, line V) is not itself the error.
- **Quantifiers:** "$\forall x\,\exists n$" lets $n$ depend on $x$; "$\exists x\,\forall n$" needs one $x$ for
  all $n$. Order is everything (2022 Q10).
- **Symmetry & substitution keep a solution-count**; an extra $\pm$ branch changes it (2023 Q6).
- **Sometimes the count is fixed:** every non-right triangle has exactly 3 such lines (2023 Q8).
- **A false statement can have a true converse** — test the converse directly (2023 Q9).
- Cross-links: **S2** (converse/contrapositive), **S4** (quantifiers), **S5/S7** (factorisation ⇒ primality,
  spot the error).
:::
